subject: Climate & Environment
title: Keystone Species
description: A quick, practical guide to Keystone Species.

hook.text: Remove one species and the whole ecosystem changes. These are called keystone species.

buildup.text: Sea otters eat sea urchins. Without otters, urchins devour kelp forests entirely.

discovery.text: Kelp forests shelter hundreds of species and absorb vast amounts of CO₂.

twist.text: When fur traders nearly wiped out otters, entire Pacific coastlines lost their kelp.

climax.text: Otter recovery brought the kelp back — and with it, fish, seals, and eagles.

punchline.text: Sometimes the smallest player holds the biggest role.

quiz.question: What happened to kelp forests when sea otters were hunted?

details.summary: A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance. Removing a keystone triggers cascading changes, such as when sea otter loss allowed urchins to destroy kelp forests along the Pacific coast.
details.whyItMatters: Keystone species show that not all species play equal ecological roles. Protecting them is one of the most efficient strategies for preserving entire ecosystems.
takeaways: Keystone species shape ecosystems far beyond their numbers
Sea otters, wolves, and elephants are classic keystone examples
Losing a keystone causes trophic cascades that reshape habitats

faq.question: How do sea otters maintain kelp forests?
faq.answer: Sea otters eat sea urchins that graze on kelp. Without otters, urchin populations explode and devour kelp forests, turning rich underwater habitats into barren urchin barrens. Restoring otters brings kelp forests back.

faq.question: What is a trophic cascade?
faq.answer: A trophic cascade occurs when changes at the top of the food chain ripple down through lower levels. Removing a top predator allows herbivore populations to surge, which overgrazes vegetation, which in turn affects soil, insects, and birds.
